subject: BRGSA
subjectTitle: Business Research and Growth Systems Architecture

sections.rule: One correct option. Two marks each. No negative marking.
A short scenario, then a task. Both parts must be right for the marks. No partial credit.
A complete structured response. Not machine-marked.

paper.stem: Which metric is least suitable for an operating decision rule?
options: Weekly activation rate by signup cohort
All-time cumulative app downloads
Contribution margin per delivered order
Day-30 repurchase rate by delivery cohort

paper.stem: A team spends ₹3,00,000 on a channel and acquires 120 paying customers attributable to it. What is channel CAC?
What makes lean validation different from simply doing more market research?
options: It always turns the demand assumption into a test whose threshold is set before any build
It replaces customer evidence with the founder's own judgment about the problem
It estimates the total addressable market from desk research before speaking to any real buyers
It begins only after the product is complete and ready to put in front of customers

paper.stem: A team sends the same weekly email to every user, regardless of their stage. What is missing?
options: Lifecycle engagement always matched to the user's current state and next value action
A substantially larger top-of-funnel for the whole team to work with each month
A greater overall volume of email being sent
A referral discount offered to every single existing user on the mailing list

paper.caselet: Users who complete a 12-step profile are retained, so the team calls profile completion the aha moment. New-user recordings show most people leave before experiencing the product's core output.
paper.stem: What is the best response?
options: Add more required profile fields in order to strengthen the user's commitment
Measure the all-time total number of profiles ever created on the product up to today
Use the count of completed profiles as the denominator for the activation metric instead of signups
Identify the first value event and define activation around it, removing every step before it that does not help

paper.stem: Why does the course call pricing a structure rather than just a number?
options: Because the published price should never be allowed to change afterwards
Because a lower headline number is always better for winning new customers more quickly
Because only the finance team is permitted to set it in the first place
Because tiers, units, limits and packaging shape every part of customer behaviour and the expansion path

paper.stem: Why is ‘Would you buy this?’ a weak primary validation question?
options: People cannot understand a product before launch
Stated intention under social pressure never reliably predicts actual purchase behaviour
Surveys always require more than a thousand responses before they mean anything
Only direct competitors are allowed to run such surveys

paper.stem: Which description best distinguishes growth from marketing and product?
options: Growth owns the whole system connecting acquisition, product value, retention and revenue, never one channel
Growth only ships product features and hands them to marketing
Growth is really just another name for the paid advertising budget and its management
Growth reports the total follower count and impressions to the leadership team each month

paper.stem: Why must a B2B pipeline define entry and exit criteria for each stage?
options: To increase the number of email opens recorded across each outreach sequence sent to the list
To make the CRM records look complete and tidy for internal reporting purposes each quarter
So conversion always reflects real buyer progress and never a subjective sales label
To avoid having to speak to customers directly at any point in the process

paper.caselet: Monthly active users rose from 10,000 to 14,000 after a large campaign. Each new signup cohort, however, retains fewer users by week four than the cohort before it.
paper.stem: What does the cohort view reveal?
options: Acquisition volume is masking deteriorating retention
Retention is improving because the total user number is larger
The campaign has proven that product-market fit exists
Cohorts cannot meaningfully be compared across time

paper.stem: What separates an organic loop from a one-off viral campaign?
options: A loop generates a larger number of impressions than a campaign
The output of every cycle becomes an input that brings or activates the next user
A loop always runs without requiring any creative work from the team at all
A campaign cannot make use of referrals in any form whatsoever

paper.stem: For an A/B landing-page test, which plain-language null hypothesis is best formed?
options: There is never a meaningful difference between A and B until the evidence is strong enough to reject that position
Both variants must receive an identical number of conversions before the test result can be considered valid at all
Variant B will definitely win once enough traffic has been sent through both of the pages being compared
The team prefers Variant A and should state that preference before the test begins

paper.caselet: A high-ACV B2B tool sells to heads of sales at 50–200 employee companies. A cheap, broad-interest video channel brings many views but almost no qualified meetings.
paper.stem: What is the core diagnosis?
options: The product clearly cannot have found product-market fit yet
All B2B products require television advertising in order to reach the relevant decision-makers at scale
The high view count is proof enough that the channel is working exactly as intended
The channel's targeting and output never match the product's economics and ICP

paper.caselet: A pricing change that genuinely improves conversion is tested on far too few users. The test reports no difference and the team drops the change.
paper.stem: What has happened, and what follows?
options: A Type I error: the test has reported a result that was not real, so the alpha level should be tightened before anyone retests it.
Neither error: the test returned the correct result for the data it had, so the decision to drop the change stands.
A measurement error: the conversion metric must have been defined inconsistently across the two groups.
A Type II error: the test was underpowered and missed a real effect, so it should be re-run with an adequate sample.

paper.stem: Which evidence should receive the greatest weight in a build/no-build decision?
options: Commitments from target customers under an offer with real terms
A large total number of advertising impressions delivered to the market so far
High levels of enthusiasm expressed in a survey
Strong founder confidence in the idea's eventual commercial success in the market

paper.stem: What keeps an ICE score from becoming a polished opinion?
options: Letting the most senior person in the room set all three of the values alone
Removing the written assumptions that sit behind each of the three scores entirely from the record
Scoring every single idea a ten on all three of the dimensions at once every time
Tying all three scores to something checkable: the constraint, the evidence, and real capacity

paper.stem: Which dashboard change most directly prevents new acquisition from hiding a retention decline?
options: Plot retention by signup cohort, since only equal age makes cohorts comparable
Remove the denominators from every chart shown on the dashboard
Show the larger total-user numbers more prominently
Combine all customers into a single blended average figure

paper.stem: Which change most clearly turns cold email activity into an outbound system?
options: Defining ICP, list quality, sequence and qualification as one repeatable flow, never as separate tactics
Counting every single email open as a genuine sales opportunity worth adding to the pipeline
Sending a much larger volume of the same generic messages out to everyone every single week
Changing the email copy every single day without ever stating a hypothesis to test first

paper.stem: Which activation metric is fully formed?
options: A running total of 4,000 activated users counted across the whole product since launch day
The users who said that they liked the onboarding experience when they were asked about it
Percentage of verified free signups who receive their first automated follow-up within 7 days
The total number of follow-up emails that the system has ever sent to anyone

paper.caselet: Two companies each average $10,000 in annual revenue per account. One charges a flat rate; the other charges per seat. A year later the second has grown revenue per account substantially and the first has not, with no change in either customer base.
paper.stem: What explains the difference?
options: The per-seat company raised its list price during the year, which the flat-rate company chose not to do.
The structures make different promises about growth: per-seat revenue grows as a customer's team grows, flat rate does not.
The per-seat company's customers were larger organisations to begin with, so the same structure produced more revenue from each of them.
The flat-rate company has better retention, which it bought by holding its price steady through the year.

paper.caselet: Two hundred people say they like the idea, thirty join a wait-list, and four accept a refundable deposit under stated terms. The founder wants to report the survey as the strongest demand signal.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)
‘A great idea’ in a survey. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)
A like on the announcement. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)
Weight every demand signal by what it cost the prospect to give, and require a real commitment before treating demand as proven. (Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: A Type I error scales something that does not work; a Type II error abandons something that does. Every test outcome lands in one of the four cells of that matrix.

Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: An experiment starts from the null position that nothing changed, and the variant earns the decision only when evidence collected to a pre-set sample is strong enough to reject it.

Pre-sales commitment and evidence strength: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.

paper.caselet: Total active users climb every month while each newer signup cohort holds fewer users at week four than the cohort before it, and the team plans to increase spend.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Cohorts and retention)
Retention is improving because the total user number is larger. (Cohorts and retention)
The campaign has proven that product-market fit exists. (Cohorts and retention)
Read retention by signup cohort and time since entry before concluding from a rising total that growth is working. (Cohorts and retention)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Cohorts and retention: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.
Cohorts and retention: A cohort groups users by when they entered so retention can be compared at equal age, which aggregate totals cannot do because they mix new arrivals with survivors.
Cohorts and retention: CAC carries no decision meaning without an estimate of the value it buys, so LTV is estimated early from observed lifespan, margin and revenue rather than waited for.
Cohorts and retention: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

paper.caselet: A high-visibility feature scores well on team enthusiasm, has no evidence behind its confidence score, needs a quarter of engineering, and does not touch the activation step the funnel math identified.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Prioritisation)
Score every candidate experiment against the current primary constraint, and cap confidence at five whenever the supporting evidence cannot be named in one sentence. (Prioritisation)
Add another forty ideas to the existing backlog list. (Prioritisation)
Run every test in parallel at the same time. (Prioritisation)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Prioritisation: A metric earns a place on the dashboard only when it carries an owner, a threshold, and an action already agreed for the moment it crosses that threshold.
Prioritisation: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Prioritisation: ICE scores each idea on impact against the current constraint, confidence backed by evidence that can be named, and ease including the time to a credible signal, turning a list of ideas into an ordered backlog.

Prioritisation: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.

paper.caselet: Registrations rise sharply after a campaign, but most users leave somewhere inside a twelve-step onboarding flow before the product has done anything for them.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Use the count of completed profiles as the denominator for the activation metric instead of signups. (Activation and onboarding friction)
Measure the all-time total number of profiles ever created on the product up to today. (Activation and onboarding friction)
Audit the whole path to first value, classify the friction at each step, and remove or defer anything that does not help the user reach it. (Activation and onboarding friction)
Apply the joining test — does one more user make the product more valuable to existing users — and run the referral playbook when the answer is no. (Activation and onboarding friction)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Activation and onboarding friction: Every channel has fixed properties — targeting, control, input cost, output quality, time to result and economics — and it fits only when those match the product's buyer and unit economics.

Activation and onboarding friction: Demand signals sit on a commitment spectrum: social engagement is the easiest to produce and the least meaningful, while a payment or signed commitment is a different category of evidence altogether.

Activation and onboarding friction: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer, and answers it before the product is built at a fraction of the cost of building it.

Activation and onboarding friction: Activation is the first observable moment a user experiences the promised value, and every step standing between signup and that moment sheds a share of the users still remaining.

paper.caselet: A grocery-delivery app works in one city, where 34% of users order weekly and unprompted word of mouth supplies 61% of new users at no acquisition cost. It launched in four more cities on the strength of that. In the new cities, 7% order weekly, word of mouth supplies 9%, and acquisition runs at ₹740 per user through discount vouchers. The single operational difference is delivery time: 24 minutes in the original city against 71 minutes in the others, where the app has no dark store and picks from partner supermarkets. A test of a daily-streak reward, modelled on a language-learning app, ran across the new cities for five weeks and showed no effect; the sample was 600 users per arm against a required 7,000, and the feature has been abandoned. Nobody has tested reducing delivery time. Groceries are bought about once a week by these users, and the original city's ordering pattern is concentrated on Saturday mornings. The team is proposing to raise voucher spend in the four cities to buy the word-of-mouth flywheel it saw at home.
paper.stem: Write the assessment of this expansion. Address the voucher proposal and the abandoned streak feature, and say what should be tested next.

paper.caselet: An exam-preparation company surveyed 600 students about a proposed ₹4,000 revision course. 71% said they would buy it, and the product was built over four months on that basis. A landing page with a stated price and a payment button has since drawn 3,100 visitors and 22 purchases. The team then tested two page designs to fix the conversion rate. Variant A ran on weekday traffic, variant B over a weekend when a competitor's discount campaign was live. The pre-calculated sample was 4,000 sessions per variant; the test was called at 1,300 sessions each because the difference looked settled, and the 2.4-point gap it reported has not appeared since. A second experiment on the checkout flow was declared a failure at 900 sessions per variant against a required 5,000, and that change was abandoned; a later engineering estimate suggested it would have been worth about ₹90 lakh annually if the effect had been real. The team is now proposing another survey, this time with 2,000 students.
paper.stem: Write the review this team needs. Name each failure precisely, and say what should happen to the proposal for a larger survey.
